quizzes.title: Act provisions check
quizzes.passage: Russia's war in Ukraine has prompted the United States to enact a law that increases economic pressure on Russia, while also extending and strengthening certain sanctions against Iran. The statute, named after Lindsey O. Graham, is built around criteria that decide which buyers of Russian energy fall within its reach. The law gives the executive branch several trade tools, including tariffs on the largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas and tariffs on goods of Russian origin. Because the list of relevant buyers can change over time, the law provides for a periodic review carried out by the trade representative. Countries that rely only lightly on Russian gas, and that are actively cutting their imports, may qualify for a special exception. The framework's effect is also conditional, since it may be affected if Russia meets certain conditions linked to peace in Ukraine and to the stance of the Ukrainian government. For India, the measure is especially relevant because the country remains one of the major buyers of Russian crude, so Indian policymakers must weigh energy security against trade relations with the United States. Its economic effects would depend on how the tariffs are applied and how buyers respond.

Select the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The Act names no country, but its criteria place major buyers such as India and China within its scope, which explains why India is affected.

III. Tariffs on Russian-origin goods   ->   C. Through 2031
IV. Extension of Iran Sanctions Act of 1996   ->   D. 180-day review cycle
questions.explanation: The review of purchasers is on a 180-day cycle, the facilitator tariffs target the Top 5, Russian-origin goods face up to 500%, and the Iran Sanctions Act runs through 2031.

questions.q:

III. A country importing less than 15% of its natural gas from Russia can qualify for an exception if it takes significant steps to reduce such imports.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statement II is wrong because the review cycle is 180 days, not 90 days.

quizzes.title: Legal tools check
quizzes.passage: Trade measures linked to Russian energy purchases raise questions about how long they will last. A measure that has been passed by the legislature and signed into federal law carries greater legal permanence. American trade policy also relies on older statutes that give the government tools to respond to foreign practices. One of these allows the trade representative to examine unfair conduct by other countries. Another permits restrictions on imports when they are seen as a risk to national security. The government has also used tariffs on certain imported metals, and it has applied tariffs connected with goods produced through forced labour. For a country like India, such instruments matter because they change the cost of exports and make trade talks more complicated. Officials and businesses often watch these tools closely because a single measure can affect many sectors at once. Understanding the legal route behind each tariff helps explain why some measures last longer than others.

questions.explanation: The text states that in February 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the broader tariff regime.

quizzes.title: Joint Commission: Practice MCQs
quizzes.passage: Pakistan and China have set up a Boundary Joint Commission to watch over how their border management arrangements are put into practice. The body is meant to help the two sides coordinate on the everyday business of a shared frontier, including joint surveys, the flow of trade across the boundary and ties between people on either side. Its roots lie in an earlier bilateral framework on managing the boundary, which laid the groundwork for the new institution. The arrangement has drawn a firm response from India, which maintains that the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are integral parts of the country. New Delhi has questioned the move and reaffirmed its own claims over the territory concerned. The dispute centres on the Shaksgam Valley, a mountainous stretch in the Karakoram region, which came under a boundary agreement signed in the 1960s. Routes and infrastructure that link Xinjiang with Pakistan add to the importance of the arrangement, because they strengthen connectivity in a sensitive part of the western Himalayas. India therefore reads the Commission as part of a wider pattern of China-Pakistan coordination close to its own northern frontiers.

questions.q: The Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission was operationalised in which month and city (inaugural meeting)?
questions.explanation: The Commission was operationalised in September 2026, with its inaugural meeting held in Islamabad.

questions.q: The Boundary Joint Commission originates from which agreement?
options: 2013 Pakistan-China Agreement on Boundary Management System
questions.explanation: The Commission originates from the 2013 Pakistan-China Agreement on Boundary Management System.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India has rejected the Pakistan-China Joint Commission insofar as it concerns territory India claims.
Reason (R): Pakistan has no locus standi to enter into arrangements involving territory India regards as under Pakistan's illegal occupation.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: India has rejected the mechanism because, in its view, Pakistan has no locus standi over territory it regards as under illegal occupation.

quizzes.title: Disputed Lines: TITA Set
quizzes.passage: The boundary between India and China has never been fully settled, and disagreements over it have produced a long chain of confrontations. Two stretches of the frontier sit at the heart of the dispute. One lies in the high region of Aksai Chin, which the two sides understand differently, each relying on its own historical line. The other involves Arunachal Pradesh, which China describes as part of Tibet while India administers it as a full state. The line in that area was agreed at a convention attended by Tibet, China and British India, but China refused to accept it, arguing that Tibet could not conclude treaties. Armed encounters and standoffs have since erupted in several places, including mountain passes in Sikkim and Arunachal and the plateau where three countries meet. A practical dividing line emerged after the war of the early 1960s, and both sides have since tried to prevent escalation through talks and confidence-building measures. Local commanders meet at designated points to resolve friction on the ground, while senior commanders negotiate withdrawals when standoffs become serious. Yet incidents continue in the high mountains. Understanding these disputed lines is therefore essential for reading news about the border, since each claim carries a long history behind it.

questions.q: China administers Aksai Chin as part of which autonomous region? (name the region)
questions.explanation: China administers Aksai Chin as part of its Xinjiang Autonomous Region.

questions.q: In which year was the McMahon Line demarcated? (year)
questions.explanation: The McMahon Line was demarcated in 1914 during the Simla Convention.

questions.q: On which date in 1962 did China unilaterally declare a ceasefire? (day and month)
questions.explanation: China unilaterally declared a ceasefire on 19 Nov 1962.

questions.q: Into how many sectors is the Line of Actual Control divided? (number)
questions.explanation: The LAC is divided into three sectors: Eastern, Middle and Western.

questions.q: Which Chinese Premier introduced the term 'Line of Actual Control' in 1959? (name)
questions.explanation: The term was introduced in 1959 by Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai.

quizzes.title: Properties of map projections
quizzes.passage: Every world map is an attempt to show a curved surface on a flat sheet, and that task cannot be done without some loss. The Earth is not a perfect sphere, and its surface is curved in every direction. Cartographers therefore use map projections, which are systematic rules for transferring the globe onto a plane. No single flat map can keep every feature of the globe correct at the same time. Mapmakers must choose which properties to protect, such as the size of landmasses, the shapes of countries, the distances between places, or the directions between them. Some maps are made to guide travellers at sea, while others serve thematic and statistical purposes, such as showing population density. A projection that works well for one purpose may mislead when used for another. Over time, different projections have been developed, each built around a different choice of property. Readers should therefore check which property a map keeps accurate before drawing conclusions about the world from its outlines. The choice of projection is a practical decision rather than a search for one perfect map.

questions.q: Which property do equal-area projections preserve?
questions.explanation: Equal-area projections preserve relative areas, as the Equal Earth projection does.

quizzes.title: Equal Earth and the Correct the Map campaign
quizzes.passage: A world map has to make choices, and the projection behind it decides which features look accurate. Many wall maps have long used a projection that suits navigation but makes landmasses far from the Equator look larger than they really are. Equal Earth is a newer world projection designed to display the entire globe while keeping the relative sizes of landmasses accurate. It avoids the severe, jarring shape distortions found in earlier equal-area maps. A campaign called Correct the Map has urged the wider use of equal-area projections, and two advocacy groups run it. Regional bodies have endorsed the idea, and the matter was taken up by the United Nations General Assembly. The resolution received wide support, but it also drew opposition and abstentions in the vote. Such a resolution carries political weight, yet it does not have binding force. Schools, publishers and governments are therefore free to decide whether to change the maps they use. Maps shape how people picture the size and position of countries. Choosing a projection is therefore a practical decision that depends on the purpose of the map. Readers should check what a map is designed to show before drawing conclusions from it. Only time will show whether the new map becomes common in classrooms and official documents.

quizzes.title: CEC Appointment and Removal: MCQ Set
quizzes.passage: The Election Commission of India is a constitutional body, placed under Part XV of the Constitution, that administers elections to Parliament, the State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice President. Its job is to ensure free and fair elections across the country. Since 1993, it has functioned as a three-member body, with one Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and two Election Commissioners (ECs). Earlier, the President made these appointments on the advice of the Prime Minister. In Anoop Baranwal vs Union of India (2023), a five-judge bench directed that the CEC and ECs be appointed on the advice of a Selection Committee. Parliament then passed the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 to comply with that directive. Under the Act, the Selection Committee consists of the Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister and the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha. A Search Committee, headed by the Minister of Law and Justice, prepares a panel of names for the Selection Committee to consider. The Opposition has recently announced plans to move a motion in Parliament seeking the removal of the CEC. This has drawn fresh attention to the constitutional safeguards that govern the independence and removal of the CEC.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

quizzes.title: Electoral Rolls and SIR: Typed Answer Set
quizzes.passage: An electoral roll is the official list of individuals eligible to vote in a given election within a specific jurisdiction, and being listed on it is a legal prerequisite for casting a vote in India. The publishing and updating of electoral rolls are the joint responsibility of the Election Commission of India, the state's Chief Electoral Officer and the state's election commission. The Commission has broad authority over voter list management, and no individual may be excluded from electoral rolls on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex. The Commission can direct a fresh revision of rolls, which may be intensive, summary or a combination of both. An intensive revision involves a complete and fresh preparation of rolls through house-to-house enumeration, and it is done when the rolls are outdated, inaccurate or need complete rebuilding. A summary revision is a routine annual updating of existing rolls, while a special revision is undertaken in exceptional cases. The Special Intensive Revision is a focused, time-bound house-to-house verification of voters by Booth Level Officers, aimed at adding missing voters, removing ineligible ones and correcting entries. Such a revision excludes non-citizens and includes citizens aged 18 or above who are ordinarily resident in the constituency. Courts have also held that names cannot be removed from voter lists merely on suspicion, and the right to vote is treated as a statutory right rather than a fundamental one.

quizzes.title: Programme 2.0 and Its Pillars
quizzes.passage: Semiconductors have become central to modern life because they power automobiles, hospitals, defence systems, aircraft, telecom networks and a wide range of consumer goods. Modern chips can hold billions of transistors within very small areas, which makes them essential for high-performance computing, artificial intelligence and digital services. Semiconductors sit at the base of the global electronics industry, a very large economic sector. The COVID-19 pandemic showed how risky it is when chip production is concentrated in a few places, and many countries have since tried to build their own capabilities. India's response is a national programme that seeks to build a complete semiconductor ecosystem, covering design, fabrication, packaging, research and skilled manpower. Its purpose is to give the sector financial and infrastructure support, so that domestic companies can grow and compete. The government hopes this will make India a dependable partner in the global value chain, in line with the vision of self-reliance and manufacturing for the world. Several areas of the programme are meant to move forward together, so that progress in design, equipment, factories and people keeps pace with one another.

quizzes.title: Schemes and Partnerships in Brief
quizzes.passage: India's push into semiconductors uses several kinds of government support rather than a single measure. Some tools are aimed at manufacturing, with financial incentives for companies that set up production within the country and attract large investments. Others are aimed at design, because a country that can design its own chips depends less on imported technology. Academic institutions and start-ups are part of this effort, as they need access to specialised resources, training facilities and design infrastructure. Research bodies are also building their own processors, including designs based on an open instruction architecture, which adds to domestic technical strength. Support for design firms is planned over a long stretch so that they can move from early development to full deployment. Diplomacy plays a role as well. India has signed a strategic technology agreement with a major economy to expand cooperation in research, business and defence industry. It has also joined a coalition of countries that wish to protect the supply of critical minerals, manufacturing capacity and digital infrastructure. Together these steps reflect an attempt to lower dependence on other countries and to become a dependable part of the global chip supply network, which matters greatly in a world where supply disruptions can hurt many industries at once.

quizzes.title: Framework and rules check
quizzes.passage: The Unified Payments Interface has grown into a large digital payment network that handles billions of transactions every month. Running such a network requires continuous spending on technology, cybersecurity, fraud prevention, server capacity and customer support. Until now, merchants have not paid any fee for UPI and RuPay transactions, which helped small businesses and informal sectors adopt digital payments. As the network expands, however, planners must decide how its upkeep should be funded. The answer proposed in the new framework is a fee on certain merchant payments, while everyday low-value transactions remain free. Officials have stressed that small merchants and ordinary users should not face additional costs. The fee is therefore aimed at larger merchant payments rather than at the many small transactions that make up daily life. Such a structure lets the payment ecosystem generate revenue that supports its own operation. Policymakers have sought a balance between funding the network and protecting the people who use it every day. UPI works in real time and around the clock, connecting individuals and merchants across banks. Its wide use has made it an important part of commerce for individuals and merchants alike. Because so many people rely on it, any change to how the network is priced affects a very large number of users and businesses.

quizzes.title: Exemptions and caps check
quizzes.passage: Digital payments work best when small transactions stay cheap for everyone who uses them. Small businesses need protection from additional payment processing costs. Policymakers have therefore tried to protect the smallest users while still asking larger participants to share the cost of running the network. The new approach separates payments into groups. Some payments remain free regardless of who sends or receives them, while others attract a charge only when they are large. Certain sectors that provide essential services are placed in a separate group, where a fixed charge per transaction applies rather than a percentage. Investments routed through mutual funds and securities are charged at a lower rate, because that rate is meant to encourage greater use of digital payments in formal financial markets. Several upper limits also protect users. A single ceiling prevents very large payments from carrying an unlimited fee, and small merchants who earn only modest amounts through QR codes each month are exempt from the charge altogether. Together, these rules aim to keep ordinary digital payments affordable while the payment infrastructure keeps growing.

quizzes.title: Finance, Trade and Customs MCQs
quizzes.passage: Financial and trade cooperation was among the most detailed areas of the 18th BRICS Summit, which India hosted in New Delhi in 2026. Member countries discussed how cross-border trade could be made less vulnerable to currency swings and to disruptions in global financial markets. A dedicated risk-focused initiative was also discussed, linked to large infrastructure projects across the Global South and to the geopolitical risks that such projects carry. Small enterprises received particular attention, since many of them need steady cash flow to run their operations and compete in international markets. Support for young companies also formed part of the discussions. On the tax and customs side, the summit focused on sharing knowledge between national tax authorities and on joint action against smuggling and illicit financial flows, while stressing that genuine trade should continue without unnecessary obstruction. The conversations also highlighted the role of new technologies and digital solutions for development. The overall message was that a more resilient financial architecture would help developing economies manage external shocks while keeping trade flowing.

quizzes.title: Agriculture, Health and Climate TITA
quizzes.passage: The 18th BRICS Summit also produced outcomes in areas that touch everyday life, including farming, public health, transport and climate. Member countries discussed how to make food supplies steadier, particularly when global prices move sharply. A proposed commodity marketplace was among the ideas, intended to make trade in farm produce among member countries more predictable. Cooperation on seeds, plant material and farm inputs was also highlighted, along with a farmer-centred framework for sharing information. In health, the focus was on promoting active living and on building support for mental well-being through shared training. Innovation in medicine was another theme, with attention to developing solutions that could be deployed widely in developing regions. On transport and logistics, members agreed to share technical knowledge about building resilient supply systems. Climate concerns were reflected in discussions about cleaner fuels for aviation, urban infrastructure able to withstand extreme weather, and the protection of natural carbon sinks such as tropical forests. Culinary exchanges were also part of the summit, with regional produce showcased to delegates. Together, these outcomes reflected an effort to link economic cooperation with practical improvements in people's livelihoods.

quizzes.title: 26th SCO Summit: MCQ set
quizzes.passage: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation has grown from a regional grouping into a wide Eurasian platform that links Central Asia, South Asia, China, Russia and Iran. Its work covers regional security, counter-terrorism, economic and connectivity cooperation, political dialogue, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges. Its leaders meet every year, and the host state rotates along with the chairmanship. The latest summit was held in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, and was chaired by the country's president. The gathering marked the organisation's 25th anniversary, and its theme focused on sustainable peace, development and prosperity. Leaders reviewed a large set of outcome documents on security, economy, energy, climate, institutional development and culture. The summit also reaffirmed the need for collective action against terrorism and adopted the main political document of the meeting. The summit also dealt with new mechanisms against drug trafficking and the financing of extremism, which the organisation treats as shared regional threats. A standing regional structure for counter-terrorism frames terror financing and radicalisation as collective concerns. The agenda also includes transport corridors and payment arrangements. Such a summit shows how the SCO tries to balance security concerns with its economic goals, while giving member states a common forum for their policies. It is a useful window into the organisation's priorities.

quizzes.title: SCO origins: typed answers
quizzes.passage: The organisation's story begins with a grouping built to settle old disputes. Its early members were mainly concerned with borders between neighbours and with building trust among their armed forces. Over time, the group admitted new members and widened its agenda from border questions to security, trade and people-to-people contact. Membership has grown in stages, and some countries first took part as observers before becoming full members. Today the organisation has a secretariat that handles routine administration, and a council of heads of state that takes the most important decisions. Its counter-terrorism work runs through a regional structure based in Uzbekistan. The chairmanship moves between member states each year, which keeps the organisation's leadership spread across the region. Its leaders also meet at the annual summit, where the chair passes from one member to the next. The organisation's objectives include strengthening mutual trust, good-neighbourliness and mutual support on security and counter-terrorism. It also aims to promote cooperation in trade, economy, connectivity, transport, digital economy and environmental protection. Over the years, members have built a shared set of institutions, and their common work is coordinated through the secretariat and the heads of state council. The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation describes its goals as peace, security, stability, economic cooperation and cultural exchange in the SCO region.

quizzes.title: UNGA, P4M and India's Stand
quizzes.passage: The 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly opened on 8 September 2026 in New York, under the theme 'Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All.' On its sidelines, India's External Affairs Minister co-chaired the inaugural Partners for Multilateralism, International Law, Peace and Prosperity (P4M) Summit with European Council President Antonio Costa. The P4M framework is built upon the Carney Doctrine on middle-power solidarity, which Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered at Davos. The initiative was conceived in response to the erosion of global consensus, trade weaponisation and escalating conflicts across Europe and West Asia. It was conceptualised by leaders of the European Union, Brazil, Kenya and Canada, and is co-sponsored by India, Australia and Barbados. It is designed as an open and flexible framework rather than another exclusive international bloc or permanent bureaucracy. It seeks to strengthen international law, peace, multilateral cooperation and inclusive prosperity, and to enable countries from different political traditions to cooperate on reforming multilateral institutions and addressing common global challenges. Meanwhile, India used the same period of diplomacy to argue for reformed multilateralism, stressing risks to supply chains, the need for more inclusive decision-making and comprehensive reform of the United Nations Security Council.

quizzes.title: Greenland and the US Agreement
quizzes.passage: Greenland, the world's largest island, lies between North America and Europe, which makes it a linchpin in Arctic and trans-Atlantic security. It is one of Denmark's two autonomous territories, and it is self-governing. Greenland lies within the GIUK gap, a strategic chokepoint for monitoring naval movements in the North Atlantic. The United States maintains Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, which is a pivotal facility for monitoring potential missile threats. A new trilateral agreement among the United States, Denmark and Greenland builds on earlier defence arrangements while recognising Greenland's right to self-determination. It provides for expanded activities at Pituffik and for US military access to Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland, along with broader operational access across Greenland's land, air and maritime areas. The agreement restricts military presence by non-NATO states through joint approval, and it does not transfer sovereignty over Greenland to the United States. Beyond security, Greenland holds large untapped reserves of rare earth minerals, and melting Arctic ice is opening new maritime corridors such as the Transpolar Sea Route. Denmark's firm stance highlights the tension between territorial sovereignty and the strategic ambitions of major powers.

quizzes.title: Reading the Index
quizzes.passage: Gender equality is often discussed in terms of laws and policies, but measuring it is a separate challenge. One widely cited tool is the Global Gender Gap Index, which is published every year as a flagship report. Its purpose is not simply to count how many women hold particular positions. Instead, it asks how far each country has moved toward closing the disparities between women and men. This focus on gaps rather than absolute outcomes shapes the whole report. Each country receives a numerical score, and these scores allow nations to be compared on a common yardstick. One end of the range signals complete equality, while the other end signals absolute inequality. The scores can also be presented on a more familiar scale, where the highest value stands for full parity. Because the report is repeated each year, observers can see whether countries are moving forward or falling behind. Readers should remember that a ranking captures relative progress among the countries covered. It does not, by itself, describe the daily experience of women in any single society. Understanding the method behind the scores is therefore as important as reading the final table.

quizzes.title: Global Progress Check
quizzes.passage: Global progress toward gender equality is measured through rankings and overall scores, and the latest edition offers a mixed picture. The top of the table has stayed remarkably stable, with the same country holding the leading position for a long stretch. Several nations close behind it have also kept strong positions. Movement at the bottom of the table is watched closely, since the lowest-ranked countries show the widest gaps. Across the world, the overall gap has narrowed, but only slightly from the previous year, which means change is slow. Leadership remains a challenge in every sphere. Women hold only a small share of chief executive roles, and their presence in emerging technology work is also limited. Career patterns add to the picture, since women are more likely than men to take breaks from work linked to parenting. One new country joined the group of top performers for the first time in this edition. Taken together, these trends suggest that closing gaps requires sustained effort rather than occasional improvement.

quizzes.title: Sarvekshan rankings check
quizzes.passage: The Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan is an annual assessment of the cities covered under the National Clean Air Programme. It was first launched in 2022-23. The cities are grouped into three categories according to their population: Category I covers the largest cities, Category II covers mid-sized cities and Category III covers the smallest cities in the assessment. The assessment focuses on seven areas of measures: road dust management, solid waste management, vehicular emissions, industrial emissions, construction and demolition waste, commercial sources, and public awareness and outreach initiatives. Cities are evaluated on five key parameters: ambient air quality, source apportionment, action plan implementation, institutional capacity and public participation. Swachh Vayu Diwas 2026 was observed on 7 September 2026, which coincides with the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies. The fifth set of Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan Awards was presented on that occasion. The awards recognise cities and wards that have shown effective air pollution mitigation measures under the programme. The 2026 edition also introduced a new feature: ward-level rankings, which show how individual wards compare with one another. City-level results are reported within each category, which means cities are compared with others of similar population.

quizzes.title: NCAP numbers check
quizzes.passage: The National Clean Air Programme is a national-level strategy launched by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change to address air pollution through coordinated interventions across sectors. It covers non-attainment cities along with million-plus cities. Non-attainment cities are those that have failed to comply with the National Ambient Air Quality Standards over a specified assessment period. Its initial target was a 20 to 30 per cent reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 concentrations by 2024. Later, the target was enhanced to a reduction in particulate matter concentration by 2026, and the revised target has not been fully achieved. Annual PM10 concentrations are compared with the base year to measure progress. Progress is also tracked through the PRANA portal, which was launched to track NCAP progress and regulate air pollution in non-attainment cities. The National Air Quality Index is a tool for communicating air quality status to people in terms that are easy to understand. The Graded Response Action Plan is a set of emergency measures that come into effect when air quality shifts from Poor to Very Poor. Other measures include the Bharat Stage VI vehicle emission standards, which replaced BS-IV norms nationwide.

quizzes.passage: Earth observation satellites help governments see what is happening on the ground without sending anyone to the site. The satellite was lifted into space by an indigenous heavy-lift rocket from an Indian launch centre, and the mission is treated as a test of the country's launch capability. The spacecraft is described as an advanced Earth observation satellite meant for continuous and high-frequency imagery. Such imagery supports disaster response, border watch and farm monitoring. As the booklet notes, the choice of orbit determines geographical coverage, image resolution, revisit time and the mission application. The same imagery can help plan emergency responses and track weather events. The sections that follow describe the satellite, the orbit it uses and the other missions that share its theme. Students preparing for competitive examinations should note that such questions usually test the specific numbers, stages and names attached to a mission, since these details are easy to confuse.

quizzes.title: NISAR radar check
quizzes.passage: The NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar satellite, called NISAR in short, is a partnership between two space agencies and is described as the first joint Earth-observation satellite of its kind between them. Conventional cameras depend on visible light, but radar works differently. A synthetic aperture radar sends microwave pulses toward the ground and builds images from the returning signals, so it can produce sharp pictures in darkness and through clouds. The satellite is meant to study changes in the solid Earth. Its images help track surface deformation, which is useful for understanding earthquakes, volcanic activity and landslides. The same data can also support monitoring of floods, biomass, deforestation, crop health and soil moisture. The booklet calls its radar technology among the finest synthetic aperture radar systems ever designed. Its large receiving antenna and wide imaging swath make it suitable for mapping large surface areas in three dimensions. Because the satellite can detect minute ground shifts, its data is used for tectonic and structural analysis.

quizzes.title: Disputes at Sea, Land and Lake
quizzes.passage:
Several disputes over sea, land and naming drew attention this month. A Pakistani naval vessel, PNS Hunain, collided with the Indian Navy warship INS Kolkata in the North Arabian Sea. India described the conduct of the Pakistani vessel as unsafe, said the incident took place in international waters, and lodged a diplomatic protest. The episode became both a maritime and a diplomatic dispute. A similar collision had taken place in the Gulf of Aden in June 2011, involving INS Godavari and PNS Babur.

The two countries already have a bilateral agreement from 1991 that is meant to reduce the possibility of accidents between their naval platforms. It is a confidence-building measure intended to prevent misinterpretation of military activities.

Elsewhere, the long-running Falklands dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom has resurfaced, with disagreements over sovereignty and oil exploration around the islands. The United Kingdom says it has exercised continuous and peaceful authority over the islands, while Argentina considers British control illegitimate and refers to the territory as Las Malvinas. The islands are a British Overseas Territory.

In North America, the United States has moved to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America. Canada opposed the proposal, pointing to the name's Indigenous Wendat origins and its long use. Lake Ontario is one of the five Great Lakes and lies between Ontario province and New York State.

quizzes.title: Economy and Schemes: Key Numbers
quizzes.passage:
Several economic and infrastructure stories were in the news this month. The Union Cabinet approved a scheme to promote new surface coal and lignite gasification projects that produce syngas, building on the National Coal Gasification Mission launched in 2021. Gasification converts coal into a gaseous fuel instead of burning it directly, and the scheme is part of a wider national objective for coal gasification capacity by 2030. Eligible projects receive financial assistance on their plant and machinery, subject to ceilings for each project, each product and each entity.

In electric mobility, NITI Aayog and World Resources Institute India released the India Electric Mobility Index 2025. It evaluates how States and Union Territories are progressing towards electric mobility on a scale of 0 to 100, using three pillars: transport electrification progress, charging infrastructure readiness and EV research and innovation. Delhi retained the highest overall position.

A long-pending inter-state project, the Kishau Multipurpose Dam, has also moved forward. It is planned on the Tons River, a tributary of the Yamuna, and several States and Union Territories have reached agreement on its implementation.

Urban statistics were discussed too. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs told a Parliamentary panel that the criteria for identifying a Census Town may no longer reflect India's changing urbanisation. A Census Town is treated as urban for Census purposes even though it may not be a formally notified urban local body.

Finally, India's foreign exchange reserves reached a record high, a rise linked mainly to inflows through RBI's concessional swap arrangements tied to FCNR(B) deposits.

questions.q: What percentage of the cost of the water component will the Union Government provide as Central Assistance for the Kishau Multipurpose Dam Project? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: The Union Government provides 90% of the cost of the water component, and the remaining 10% is shared by the participating States/UT.

questions.q: Up to what percentage of expenditure on plant and machinery will the government provide as financial assistance under the new coal and lignite gasification scheme? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: The booklet states that the government will provide financial assistance of up to 20% of expenditure on plant and machinery.

questions.q: How many performance indicators does the India Electric Mobility Index 2025 use to evaluate States and Union Territories?
questions.explanation: The index is evaluated on a 0-100 scale across 16 performance indicators.

questions.q: How many States/UTs are participating in the Kishau Multipurpose Dam Project?
questions.explanation: The booklet lists six participating States/UT: Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Rajasthan.

questions.q: What minimum population must a settlement have to qualify as a Census Town under the criteria introduced for the 1981 Census? (in persons)
questions.explanation: A Census Town must have at least 5,000 persons, along with an occupational and a population density condition.

questions.q: After the recent rise, what global rank did India attain in foreign exchange reserves? (ordinal)
questions.explanation: India moved to 4th position globally, ahead of Russia and after China, Japan and Switzerland.

questions.q: What weight, in per cent, does the Transport Electrification Progress pillar carry in the India Electric Mobility Index 2025? (in per cent)
questions.explanation: The transport electrification pillar carries 50% of the index, with charging infrastructure at 30% and EV research and innovation at 20%.

quizzes.title: Blue Bonds and the Navier-Stokes Claim
quizzes.passage:
Financial markets are looking beyond conventional projects towards the health of the seas and rivers. A new category of debt instrument is emerging to pay for work that keeps marine and freshwater ecosystems usable and protected over the long term. India plans to join this market through a bond issued by a company that focuses on the maritime sector. The bond will be arranged by a bank's capital markets arm, which has been appointed as arranger. Governments elsewhere have already experimented with similar tools, so the idea is not entirely new.

Science also produced a headline this month. A technology company said that an advanced artificial intelligence model had produced a proposed solution to a long-standing puzzle about how fluids move. Such claims are checked with formal tools that test every step of an argument. The puzzle concerns the equations that describe the motion of water, air and honey, and it belongs to a small group of famous challenges that a mathematics institute has highlighted.

Those equations are not merely theoretical. Engineers rely on them when they design aircraft and automobiles, and scientists use them to predict weather and model currents in the ocean. Progress on the puzzle would therefore matter far beyond mathematics.

quizzes.title: Mokha Capture and Red Sea Stakes (MCQ)
quizzes.passage:
Yemen is experiencing a renewed round of fighting, and one recent development has drawn wide attention across the region. The Houthis, an Iran-aligned armed group in Yemen, have captured the strategic port town of Mocha, also written as Mokha, on the Red Sea coast. The capture expands Houthi control along Yemen's western coastline and marks a significant development in the country's conflict.

The event also affects Yemen's civil war more broadly. Strategically, Houthi control of Mocha strengthens the group's position in the area and could increase its leverage over regional maritime traffic. The Houthis emerged as an opposition movement during the 2000s, and they are also part of the Iranian-led Axis of Resistance. They are opposed to Israel and the United States.

The movement's current leader is Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, and the capital, Sanaa, is currently under Houthi control. The government that the Houthis oppose is internationally recognised, and its president is Rashad al-Alimi. The group's control of the port also fits into the wider pattern of Houthi expansion in western Yemen.

The development has implications that go beyond Yemen. Tensions involving Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Iran and other regional powers may intensify, and the events could affect global trade, energy security and Red Sea maritime security.

quizzes.title: Yemen's North-South Divide (MCQ)
quizzes.passage:
Yemen has long been divided between its north and south. The two regions have distinct religious traditions, social structures and systems of governance, and these differences were reinforced by foreign influence and colonial legacies, particularly in the south. The divide is a long-standing feature of Yemen's politics.

The Cold War era also left a lasting mark, because each part of the country was shaped by outside powers during that period. Many of the divisions that exist today can be traced back to the way the two regions developed.

Southern discontent has surfaced repeatedly in the years since. The Southern Movement, known as Al-Hirak, continues to demand greater autonomy or independence for southern Yemen, and the south remains an important part of the country's internal divisions.

A separate council in the south, the Southern Transitional Council, also seeks autonomy or independence. Recent developments show that southern politics is linked with regional powers, which back different groups in the south. Yemen's internal divisions therefore remain relevant to understanding the country today. Yemen's north and south developed separate governance systems, and the booklet links these differences to the country's modern politics. This is why the divide is still discussed in the booklet's account of Yemen's internal divisions.

quizzes.passage:

quizzes.title: Court of Arbitration findings: MCQ
quizzes.passage:
The Court of Arbitration, which sits in The Hague, examined a dispute over the Indus Waters Treaty. The dispute followed India's decision to place the treaty in abeyance after the April 2025 Pahalgam terror attack. The case raised a basic legal question: can one party step away from a treaty because of a security crisis, or must the treaty's own terms and the wider law of treaties decide the matter?

The ruling turned on the text of the treaty. The tribunal looked at the provisions on the Western Rivers, the rivers whose waters are central to the case. It also examined whether the treaty has any rules on terrorism or the use of force, since those issues sat in the background of the dispute.

The ruling also concerned a hydroelectric project on the Chenab. The tribunal placed interim limits on certain work at one of these projects, the Ratle project. Those limits are tied to a later stage of the dispute, which involves a technical expert appointed under the treaty.

India has not accepted the ruling. Its government says the tribunal was constituted improperly and has no authority over its sovereign decisions or its projects on the western rivers. The disagreement therefore covers both the substance of the treaty and the legitimacy of the forum that decided it.

questions.q: Which 1969 convention did the tribunal apply in holding that India's abeyance decision was not permissible?

questions.explanation: The ruling applied the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 1969 when holding the abeyance impermissible.

questions.q: Article III(1) of the Indus Waters Treaty obliges India to let flow the waters of which rivers to Pakistan?

questions.explanation: Article III(1) obliges India to let the waters of the Western Rivers flow to Pakistan.

questions.q: What do the tribunal's interim limits on the Ratle project bar?
options: All hydropower generation at the project
Concreting of specified parts of the dam wall and power intake beyond prescribed levels
Any release of water into the Chenab
Any survey work for future projects
questions.explanation: The interim limits bar concreting specified parts of the dam wall and power intake beyond prescribed levels.

questions.q:
Read the assertion and reason below.
Assertion (A): The tribunal held that India's decision to place the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance was not permissible.
Reason (R): The treaty gives India no unilateral mechanism to suspend its treaty obligations.
options: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

quizzes.title: Court of Arbitration findings: TITA
quizzes.passage:
A ruling from an international Court of Arbitration has placed the Indus Waters Treaty at the centre of a fresh dispute between India and Pakistan. The treaty has governed the sharing of the Indus river system since 1960, and the question now is whether India could suspend it after a security crisis in 2025. The case asks whether a treaty can be set aside on that basis, or whether it keeps applying until the parties end it through a formal agreement.

The tribunal read the treaty as written and tested India's position against the wider law of treaties. It also considered whether the treaty's text deals with the use of force. These points matter because the answer shapes how the treaty's obligations on the Western Rivers are understood. The ruling is therefore a test of how the treaty's text applies to a new situation.

The ruling also touched on the Ratle project, a hydroelectric scheme in Jammu and Kashmir. Interim limits were placed on some work there, and those limits remain linked to a later stage of the dispute.

quizzes.title: India's objection to the tribunal: MCQ
quizzes.passage:

Its rules cover how the waters are shared, and it also sets out how disagreements are to be handled. That second part has become the focus of a recent dispute, because India has rejected a ruling from an international tribunal and has questioned whether the tribunal should have been formed at all.

The debate turns on the structure of the treaty. The two countries read its disputes process differently, and the answer affects which forum can hear a particular question. Each reading leads to a different view of whether the tribunal had any role to play. Both sides refer to the same treaty text, and they differ in how they read it. This difference in reading is at the heart of the dispute.

Parallel moves also matter. In the years before the ruling, both sides pursued processes at the same time, and the institutions involved had to decide how those processes could coexist. That history has given the dispute a procedural side, separate from the questions about water.

India's objections therefore concern procedure, legitimacy and the reach of the tribunal, rather than the flow of the rivers themselves.

quizzes.title: Indus river system: MCQ
quizzes.passage:
The Indus river system is one of the great river systems of South Asia, and its waters are shared by more than one country. The system is made up of a main river and several large tributaries, and each of these rises in a different part of the mountains. Some tributaries begin in high passes and glaciers, while others rise from springs in valleys below.

Because the rivers cross political borders, the way their waters are used is a matter of law as well as geography. Over time, countries and international bodies have developed rules on how shared waters should be managed. These rules cover the use of water in a shared basin and the wider conduct of states that share a watercourse.

The Indus Waters Treaty divides the rivers into two groups, and each group carries different rights for India. The eastern rivers are open to Indian use, while the western rivers are allocated primarily to Pakistan. India keeps some rights over the western rivers, subject to the treaty's conditions.

The booklet describes each river by its sources and by the points where it joins another river. The main tributaries named in the booklet are the Jhelum, the Chenab, the Ravi, the Beas and the Satluj, and each has its own course.

A trans-boundary river system needs rules that every country sharing it can accept. The Indus is one of the most significant examples in South Asia, and its basin is shared by several countries. Its main river rises far to the north, and several large tributaries join it from different directions across the region.

The tributaries have their sources in different places. Some begin in high mountain passes and frozen ice fields, while others come from springs or lakes in the mountains. As they flow, they meet one another at points along the plains, and some of these meeting points lie in Punjab.

Legal thinking about shared rivers developed over several decades. Early work set out principles for the use of water in a shared drainage basin. Later agreements dealt with other concerns, as well as with the wider law governing the non-navigational use of international watercourses.

Not every country has joined the most widely discussed of these agreements. The status of signatures shows which states have accepted the broader framework and which have stayed outside it. The main rivers of the system, including the Jhelum, the Chenab, the Ravi, the Beas and the Satluj, each have their own sources and meeting points.

quizzes.title: Devolution and the Asymmetric UK Framework
quizzes.passage:
Devolution is a feature of the constitutional arrangements of the United Kingdom. Under it, powers move from the central government to institutions below the national level, yet the centre continues to hold ultimate constitutional authority. Three territories of the UK have such institutions: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Their powers are not identical, because the extent and nature of what each can do differ. For this reason the framework is often described as asymmetric.

Wales has its own legislature, which was created by a law passed in 1998. Scotland's parliament was created by another law of the same year. Money is also part of the picture. The sums given to devolved administrations change according to a formula applied by one central department. Questions about how resources are allocated therefore form part of wider debates on the country's fiscal and constitutional arrangements.

Recently, a law was passed to regulate the domestic market across the UK after the country left the European Union. Its effects on devolved governments have been debated. These are matters that continue to be discussed across the UK. The relationship between Westminster and the devolved administrations is central to this discussion. Different parts of the country have reached different views on these questions.

quizzes.title: Good Friday Agreement and Northern Ireland
quizzes.passage:
The Good Friday, or Belfast, Agreement was a landmark accord for Northern Ireland. It was reached to bring an end to a long period of violence that had divided its people for decades. The agreement set up a system of government in which power would be shared, rather than held by one side alone. It also addressed questions of identity, and it sought to make the border between Northern Ireland and the Republic far less visible. Freedom of movement across the islands was encouraged as part of the settlement. The region's politics has been shaped by the division between those who wish to remain in the UK and those who want a united Ireland.

Its effects have been tested since. When the United Kingdom left the European Union, Northern Ireland found itself with a land border with an EU member state. Checks were then placed between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and this became a matter of dispute in the region. Political deadlock followed the 2022 election, when a government could not be formed for a time. The UK Government later published a new arrangement to address the problems that had emerged. The Good Friday Agreement remains the reference point for these questions. A border poll is one of the mechanisms the agreement provides for future constitutional change.

Its main purpose was to create a government in which people with differing views on the region's future would share power. quizzes.title: Sanctioning Russia Act: Scope and Review
quizzes.passage:
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 is a law that the United States has enacted. The measure followed Senate approval and House passage, and it was then signed by the President. Its main aim is to increase economic pressure on Russia, and it also extends and strengthens certain sanctions against Iran. The Act targets political, financial, energy and commercial networks linked to Russia's war in Ukraine. It is now federal law with greater legal permanence.

The Act's criteria bring major buyers of Russian oil and gas within its scope. India is one such buyer because it remains one of the major buyers of Russian crude. Tariffs under the Act can fall on the largest purchasers of Russian energy and on facilitators of Russian oil sanctions evasion. Certain goods of Russian origin may also face tariffs, subject to specified exceptions.

The list of relevant purchasers is not fixed. It is reviewed periodically, in consultation with other senior officials. Countries that import only a small share of their natural gas from Russia can qualify for an exception if they take significant steps to reduce such imports. The sanctions framework may also be affected if certain conditions relating to the war are met.

quizzes.title: Sanctions Act: India and Global Oil

The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 was enacted by the United States in September 2026. The Act is aimed mainly at economic pressure on Russia over the war in Ukraine, and it also strengthens certain sanctions against Iran. Its criteria place major buyers of Russian energy within its scope. The measure was passed by Congress and signed into federal law, which gives it greater legal permanence. It follows an earlier punitive tariff on India for buying Russian oil. The authorisation covers tariffs on major purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas.

India remains one of the major buyers of Russian crude, so the measure matters for India's energy planning. Russia is a major source of India's oil, and the country depends on imports to meet a large part of its energy demand. This makes the measure significant for India.

The measure reflects a broader pattern in which tariffs and sanctions are used to shape the conduct of other countries. Crude oil is traded in a connected global market.

quizzes.passage: India and China share a long frontier that runs along the Himalayan range. Much of this frontier is not a settled international boundary, and the working line between the two sides is called the Line of Actual Control. It is described as an effective military border that separates Indian-controlled areas from those held by China. Officials describe the LAC as a practical boundary rather than a legally recognised one. The frontier passes through several Indian states and one Union Territory, and each stretch has its own terrain and local conditions. India administers Arunachal Pradesh as a full-fledged state with established government institutions and civil administration. For management purposes, the LAC is divided into sectors so that officials can focus on a defined stretch. In 1954, India and China signed the Panchsheel Agreement, and its principles included a pledge by both sides to respect each other's sovereignty and territorial integrity. The slogan Hindi-Chini Bhai Bhai captured the mood of mutual trust at that time. The LAC took its practical shape after the 1962 Sino-Indian War, when a ceasefire left each side in control of different areas. Since then, both countries have used a range of mechanisms to manage incidents along the line while the wider question remains open.

quizzes.passage: The boundary between India and China follows the high Himalayan range, and much of it has not been settled by a final agreement. quizzes.title: Border Management Mechanisms and Agreements
quizzes.passage: India and China have not reached a final settlement of their boundary dispute, which covers a frontier of 3,488 km along the Himalayan range. Instead, the two sides manage the Line of Actual Control through a layered set of meetings and agreements. Those meetings take place at several levels, from senior government representatives to local officers who work along the line. Military officers also take part in talks when tensions rise, and their discussions are aimed at calming the situation on the ground. Several agreements were signed from the 1990s onward, adding further rules to the arrangement. A later agreement aimed to strengthen communication between the border forces of the two countries. The arrangement has grown over several decades, and each step has added a channel or a rule rather than settling the question. The frontier is also divided into sectors for management purposes, so that each stretch can be discussed separately. The line itself is a practical boundary rather than a legally recognised international border, so these arrangements matter for daily management. Because the frontier is long and varied, managing it is a continuing task. Together, these tools help keep the frontier calm while the wider dispute remains open.

quizzes.title: Mercator Projection: Shape, Size and Grid
quizzes.passage: Turning the round surface of the Earth into a flat map always involves some distortion. Different projections handle this in different ways, and the Mercator design is one of the most familiar. On the Mercator grid, longitudes are evenly spaced, but the gaps between latitudes widen as one moves towards the Poles. This spacing is a deliberate feature of the design, and it keeps the shapes of landmasses locally recognisable. The trade-off is that landmasses far from the Equator appear much larger than they really are, so the amount of exaggeration depends on how far a landmass lies from the Equator. Africa, for example, looks similar in size to Greenland on such a map, even though the two differ greatly in reality. Antarctica is also drawn far larger than its true size. On a standard wall map, India looks like a middleweight beside Scandinavia, which shows how much the grid can change the impression of a country's size. The Equal Earth projection is a newer design, used for thematic maps, that aims to show the whole globe in a more balanced way. Choosing a projection depends on what a map is meant to show, and each design makes its own choices about which features to keep.

questions.explanation: The Mercator projection does not preserve relative area, while the exact matching of stretching is a true property of the grid.

quizzes.title: Other Projections and Mapping in India
quizzes.passage: Map projections are not a single fixed method, and cartographers have produced many of them over time. Every flat map is a trade-off, because a flat sheet cannot match the curved surface of the globe in every respect. The Winkel Tripel was designed to reduce distortion across area, distance and direction together, instead of perfecting one property at the cost of the others. It belongs to a wider group of compromise designs, which spread errors across several properties rather than concentrating them in one. Major institutions, including a large geographic society and the World Bank, later adopted it for their maps. Such compromise maps are used for general reference and world maps, where a natural-looking view of the whole globe is useful. Choosing a projection depends on the purpose of the map, so a design that suits one task may be poor for another. Accuracy matters in official mapping for a different reason. The Survey of India is a national body that works on official maps, and among its tasks is establishing geodetic reference frameworks, which give surveys a common base. The same survey body also checks how international borders appear on published maps. Maps published in India are also subject to legal rules that control how borders may be shown.

quizzes.title: Status and Powers of the Election Commission
quizzes.passage: The Election Commission of India is a permanent, all-India and independent body that conducts elections across the country. Its basic task is to ensure that elections to the Lok Sabha, the Rajya Sabha and the State Legislative Assemblies are free and fair, and it also oversees the elections of the President and the Vice President. Since 1993, the Commission has been a three-member body. It consists of one Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners, who together carry out its work. The Commission shares responsibility for electoral rolls with the state chief electoral officers and state election commissions. An electoral roll is the official list of people eligible to vote in a given election within a specific area, and being on that list is a legal requirement for casting a vote. Its work involves preparing voter lists and managing polls, and it also has functions that the Constitution and the courts have helped to define. Because its powers are rooted in the Constitution, the Commission is described as a constitutional body. Its members also enjoy fixed service conditions that cannot be varied to their disadvantage after appointment.

quizzes.title: The EVM and the VVPAT
quizzes.passage: The Electronic Voting Machine, known as the EVM, is an electronic device that records votes in place of the traditional ballot papers and ballot boxes. The machine has been used in elections to the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and by-elections, and it has been in use across different parts of the country for several decades. Since it is electronic, votes are stored in the machine rather than being collected and counted manually from paper. A companion system, the Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail, is attached to the EVM and is meant to give voters a way to check their choice. The system is described as an independent unit that works alongside the EVM. The purpose of this arrangement is to increase confidence in the voting process among voters and political parties alike. Courts have also commented on the role of such systems in elections, and several judgments have discussed them. The overall aim is to make the physical record of each vote available for verification. Its use expanded gradually over the following years, and it was extended to elections across the country.

quizzes.title: The EVM and the VVPAT (Fill-in)
quizzes.passage: The Electronic Voting Machine, known as the EVM, is an electronic device that records votes in place of the traditional ballot papers and ballot boxes. The machine has been used in elections to the Lok Sabha, State Legislative Assemblies and by-elections, and it has been in use across different parts of the country for several decades. Since it is electronic, votes are stored in the machine rather than being collected and counted manually from paper. A companion system, the Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail, is attached to the EVM and is meant to give voters a way to check their choice. The system is described as an independent unit that works alongside the EVM. The purpose of this arrangement is to increase confidence in the voting process among voters and political parties alike. Courts have also commented on the role of such systems in elections, and several judgments have discussed them. The overall aim is to make the physical record of each vote available for verification. Its use expanded gradually over the following years, and it was extended to elections across the country.

quizzes.title: Why Semiconductors Matter: MCQ
quizzes.passage: Semiconductors are fundamental to modern technological systems, and they are built into a wide range of products. Automobiles and healthcare equipment are two of the many areas that depend on them, and consumer electronics relies on them as well. Because so much of modern life depends on these components, their availability shapes how resilient digital and industrial supply chains can be. Chip design has advanced to the point where a single chip can hold billions of transistors packed into an extremely small area. The most advanced processors use very fine manufacturing technology and can integrate a very large number of transistors. Such capability supports demanding workloads and advanced digital applications. The electronics industry that these chips serve is very large, and semiconductors form part of its base in modern technology. The way production is organised has also been questioned. Past disruptions showed how much risk comes from relying on a small number of places for supply. In response, many governments have looked for ways to build their own chip-making strength and to draw components from a wider set of sources.

quizzes.title: SEMICON India and the Programme: MCQ
quizzes.passage:
SEMICON India is a conference and exhibition that showcases India's semiconductor capabilities. It gives the sector one place to display its progress, and each edition is an occasion to present the work done in chip-related fields. The event is staged alongside the national effort to build a domestic base for chips, which the government has pursued through a dedicated programme. Its organisation involves the India Semiconductor Mission, which serves as the nodal body for the schemes in this area. The gathering brings together displays of work from across the sector, which makes it a useful window into the country's chip-related strengths.

The Semicon India Programme is the central scheme behind this effort. Its objective is to establish a complete set of capabilities in the country, running from the creation of designs through to the production and packaging of chips. The programme's work is grouped into several connected areas, and it also covers the training of skilled people and the support of research and new ideas.

Several projects have already been announced, with companies planning facilities in different parts of the country. Some of these projects involve partnerships between Indian companies and overseas firms, and they show how the programme's goals are being turned into physical units. The projects are spread across several states and cover different stages of chip making.

quizzes.title: Why the MDR framework was introduced
quizzes.passage: Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has grown into a large digital payment infrastructure that handles billions of transactions every month. As the network expands, it serves more users and more transactions, and its server capacity and customer support must keep pace. To meet these needs, the National Payments Corporation of India introduced a Merchant Discount Rate framework for certain UPI transactions. The framework gives the payment ecosystem a revenue mechanism of its own. The zero-MDR policy, introduced in 2020, had exempted merchants from paying any fee for UPI and RuPay transactions to encourage digital adoption, particularly among small traders and informal sectors. The new framework is designed so that everyday low-value transactions remain free, and the government and the payments body have both emphasised protecting small merchants and ordinary users from additional costs. Essential services such as railways, telecom, insurance and fuel are treated separately under the framework. Capital markets also receive a separate treatment. The booklet presents the framework against this background of network growth, and readers should look at its reasons as well as its rates to understand why it was introduced.

quizzes.title: Reasons behind the MDR framework
quizzes.passage: The network behind UPI handles a very large number of payments each month, and that volume keeps growing. Growth of this kind places heavy demands on the systems that run the network. Equipment and software must be upgraded regularly, and server capacity must expand as more users join. Customer support also has to be maintained for a large base of users. Fraud and other threats appear as digital payments become more common, so the operators must watch for them constantly. The Merchant Discount Rate framework was introduced to address these demands. It creates a revenue source inside the payment ecosystem. Before the framework, the zero-MDR policy had allowed merchants to accept UPI and RuPay payments without any fee, an arrangement that encouraged digital adoption among small traders and informal sectors. Under the new framework, everyday low-value transactions remain free, and the government and the National Payments Corporation of India have stressed the need to protect small merchants and ordinary users from additional costs. The framework is therefore presented as a way to sustain the network while keeping daily payments affordable for people who use them.

Keeping such a network working smoothly is a continuing task, and the booklet describes several areas that need attention as it grows. The framework discussed in the booklet applies to merchant payments above a certain value and treats some sectors separately. Readers who want to understand it should look at its slabs, its exemptions and the reasons behind it.

quizzes.title: UPI, MDR and NPCI terms

The fee falls on the business that receives the money, while the framework for it is designed around a few value slabs. The revenue from these fees stays within the network and helps support its work. Among the countries listed as accepting the system are several in Asia, along with a small number of other nations on different continents. The network is operated by a body whose functions include developing and operating payment systems across the country. Many small businesses and informal sectors were encouraged to adopt digital payments in earlier years, when merchants paid no fee at all. The booklet presents the framework as one that fits into the wider payment ecosystem and protects ordinary users from additional costs. quizzes.title: BRICS 2026 Summit Overview
quizzes.passage: India hosted the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi in 2026, a year in which the country held the grouping's chairship for the fourth time. The chairship ran under the theme 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability.' The 2026 calendar also included several ministerial and sectoral meetings held in different Indian cities. The meetings covered urbanisation, energy, transport, friendship between cities and the work of chief justices. The programme of meetings ran across several months of the year, with dates spread from June to September 2026. The host cities listed for these meetings span more than one Indian state. Each meeting formed part of India's role as chair, which covered financial, scientific, health and security cooperation among member countries. The outcomes were grouped under several headings. These included financial, economic and trade cooperation, taxation and customs cooperation, agriculture and food security, health and medicine, transport, logistics and climate cooperation, security, law and social cooperation, culinary diplomacy, and geopolitical mandates with global governance. India also showcased regional products during the summit itself, as part of its culinary diplomacy. The year also marked 25 years since the BRIC concept first emerged. quizzes.title: SCO membership and bodies
quizzes.passage: The SCO brings together a group of countries that sit at the crossroads of Central Asia, South Asia and East Asia. Russia and Iran also take part in its work, which gives the grouping a wide geographical reach. The organisation runs cooperation programmes in several areas, including security, trade, transport and cultural contacts. Its work is spread across a set of bodies, and each body handles a separate part of the agenda. The organisation's leaders meet every year, and the host country for that meeting rotates along with the chairmanship. The organisation marked its 25th anniversary in 2026, and its theme for that year stressed sustainable peace, development and prosperity. Over time, the membership has expanded in stages, and the organisation has brought in new partners as its reach has grown. The SCO also encourages political dialogue among its members and supports exchanges between the peoples of the region. Together, these features show a grouping that combines security concerns with economic and cultural work across a large part of the continent. Its members include several large states, and its meetings give them a regular channel for discussion at the highest political level. One of its stated objectives is to strengthen mutual trust, good-neighbourliness and mutual support on issues of security.

quizzes.title: SCO structure and timeline
quizzes.passage: The SCO links a broad group of Eurasian states, with members drawn from Central Asia, South Asia, China, Russia and Iran. Its agenda is wide and covers security questions, economic and connectivity projects, political dialogue, and exchanges between cultures and peoples. Leaders gather at an annual summit, and the host role moves to a different member state as the chairmanship rotates. Governance is spread across several bodies, and each has a distinct area of work. The organisation marked its 25th anniversary in 2026, and its theme for that year stressed sustainable peace, development and prosperity. Membership has grown in stages since the early years, with new countries joining at different times. The organisation's cooperation is organised around clear goals, including trust among members, trade and connectivity, and cultural exchange. Taken together, these features describe a platform that brings governments from several parts of the continent into a common framework for cooperation. Its stated objectives include strengthening mutual trust, good-neighbourliness and mutual support on issues of security. The organisation also promotes people-to-people exchange in fields such as culture, education and science. Its cooperation extends to transport and digital economy, as well as environmental protection. Its work on energy is also part of its agenda.

quizzes.title: India's SCO engagement
quizzes.passage: India's engagement with the SCO is part of its wider effort to stay active across the Eurasian region. The grouping gives India a multilateral platform where it can meet Russia and China along with several Central Asian republics. India's stated position is that peace, security and stability in the region matter, and that disputes should be settled through dialogue and diplomacy. It also supports inclusive economic development, and it highlights digital cooperation, energy partnerships and green development. India also emphasises people-to-people contacts and cultural linkages with partners. India condemns terrorism in all its forms and supports zero tolerance against it. India's approach allows it to cooperate on issues where its interests align with others while keeping room for independent choices in other matters. The grouping's stated aims include peace, security, stability, economic cooperation and cultural exchange. Its objectives also include building a just, democratic and rational new international order. The SCO is also described as a platform for cooperation, with a focus on peace, prosperity and sustainable development. The SCO allows issue-based alignment, so partners can cooperate on specific questions while differing on others. Such alignment lets India engage with Russia and China on some matters while pursuing its own position on others.

quizzes.title: India's SCO ties and outreach
quizzes.passage: India's SCO engagement sits within a broader approach to Eurasia, where access and connectivity matter. Central Asia is landlocked, so institutional links with the region carry particular weight. Energy is another part of the picture, with long-term access to key resources treated as a strategic concern. India's approach also includes cultural outreach aimed at building people-centric ties. The grouping's stated aims include peace, security, stability, economic cooperation and cultural exchange in the region. Digital governance is another area where India's rights-based approach sits in tension with the grouping's focus on data surveillance. Some frictions in the region involve the close ties between two neighbouring countries, and such issues can slow down projects. Practical progress on payment arrangements and transport corridors has been slower than the size of the grouping might suggest. The SCO allows issue-based alignment, so partners can cooperate on specific questions while differing on others. The grouping's agenda covers security, economic and connectivity cooperation, political dialogue, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges. Yet cooperation continues on several fronts, including energy partnerships and green development. The grouping's wider agenda also covers energy, transport, digital economy and environmental protection. India's commitment to peace and stability is stated clearly in its participation, which emphasises dialogue and diplomacy for resolving disputes.
